title: Регистрация Шефа в соцсети  (Registering the Chef on Social Media)

segments.t: In the office, Max pulls up Elena's profile on a social network and shows Chef Barinov the admiring comments under her photos. When Max offers to create an account for him so he can message her online, Barinov kicks him out and declares that real men ask women out the old-fashioned way.
Так я знал, что ей понравится.
Подробностях. Так я знал.
Я же сказал, медленно и в подробностях.
Да не вопрос.
Социальная сеть.
А вот комментарий к ее фотографиям.
Баран. Вообще-то он.
Шеф, хотите я вас зарегистрирую?
Баран. Шеф?
На свидание пригласите по сети, а?
Второй пошел вон за полдня.
Ни сети.
Женщин надо приглашать на свидание старым дедовским способом.
Right, let's take their exchange slowly and unpack the Russian.
Так я знал, что ей понравится.
'I knew she would like it.' Notice the reflexive suffix on the verb meaning 'will please', turning the action back on the subject.
Подробностях. Так я знал.
'In full detail. Just as I knew.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'detail' before landing on 'knew'.
Я же сказал, медленно и в подробностях.
'I told you, slowly and in full detail.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'I' and finishing on 'detail'. Max answers right away.
Да не вопрос.
'No problem at all.' The grammar packs 'yes' and 'question' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
Социальная сеть.
'It is a social network.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'social' and finishing on 'net'.
А вот комментарий к ее фотографиям.
'And here is a comment under her photographs.' Nastya brings out the contrast between 'and' and 'there you go' in a few short words. Max answers right away.
Баран. Вообще-то он.
'What a sheep. Actually, he is.' The meaning hinges on 'sheep' working together with 'he' in spoken Russian.
Шеф, хотите я вас зарегистрирую?
'Chef, would you like me to register an account for you?' Chef Viktor chooses the respectful plural 'you' alongside 'to register' to keep a polite distance.
Баран. Шеф?
'A sheep. Chef?' Notice how Russian expresses 'sheep' and 'chef' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Max answers right away.
На свидание пригласите по сети, а?
'You can ask her out on a date online, huh?' In Russian, the idea of 'on' flows naturally into 'and' without extra filler words.
Второй пошел вон за полдня.
'That is the second 'get out' in half a day.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'second' before landing on 'half a day'.
Ни сети.
'Not on any network.' The grammar packs 'no' and 'nets' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Max answers right away.
Женщин надо приглашать на свидание старым дедовским способом.

'You have to ask women out on a date the good old-fashioned way.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'women' and finishing on 'way'. Now let's listen to the entire scene again without interruption.
